extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, narratology students, and creative writers interested in narrative theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and distinguish narrative levels (extradiegetic, diegetic, metadiegetic), narrator functions, and voice (homodiegetic/heterodiegetic), including phenomena like metalepsis and pseudo-diegesis. Applies to evaluating how stories are told and how narrative acts interact with story events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diegetic / Metadiegetic / Extradiegetic distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms such as diegetic, metadiegetic, intradiegetic, extradiegetic designate relative situations and functions (narrative levels), not particular individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify for each narrating instance whether it functions at the extradiegetic (outside the story being told), diegetic (inside that story), or metadiegetic (a story within the story) level. Examples: Des Grieux as narrator at the 'Lion d'or' is diegetic/intradiegetic, whereas Des Grieux as hero of his own narrative is metadiegetic. Remember: the possibly fictive or 'real' nature of an instance does not change its narrative level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrating instance vs literary (author) instance
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the narrating instance (the enunciator who tells) from the literary or 'real' author; narrating instance's level is what matters for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat figures like 'M. de Renoncourt' or 'Robinson Crusoe' as author-narrators at the same narrative level as their public; do not conflate the historical author (Prevost, Defoe) with the narrating instance. Focus analysis on narrating instance position (extradiegetic vs diegetic), not on outside authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extradiegetic narrating need not address a public or be written
rubrics_metrics.description: An extradiegetic narrating instance is by definition outside the narrated world but may not function as a conventional 'author addressing readers'; diaries, single-letter epistolary forms, or interior monologues complicate the assumption of a public addressee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume extradiegetic = editorial/public voice. Treat diary-form or epistolary monody as extradiegetic narrating that may lack an intended public or recipient; interior monologues (stream of consciousness) may preclude formal determination of narrating instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intradiegetic narrating can take multiple media/forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrating instance inside the diegesis (intradiegetic) can present its narrative orally, as written text, as inward narration (dreams, recollection), or as a nonverbal representation converted into narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an embedded narrative, note its medium: spoken report, memoir-with-no-recipient, fictional text-within-text, dream-recollection, or visual/iconographic material described by a narrator or another character (e.g., tapestry, print). This affects focalization, epistemic access, and realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type I relationship: causal/explanatory link between metadiegesis and diegesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The metadiegetic narrative explains or causally connects prior events to the present diegetic situation (the 'this is why' function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify metadiegetic episodes that answer 'What events led to the present situation?' (examples: many Balzacian insertions, Ulysses' narrative in Odyssey Books IX–XII). Note that the metadiegetic narration often serves the reader's curiosity as much as the intradiegetic listener's and may introduce cognitive transformations rather than altering diegetic events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type II relationship: thematic (contrast/analogy) relation
rubrics_metrics.description: The metadiegetic narrative bears a thematic relationship (analogy or contrast) to the diegetic situation without spatio-temporal continuity; can function as exemplum or persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect analogical or contrastive insertions (en abyme, parable, apologue) that influence characters or audience by illustrating, persuading, or providing moral/interpretive models (examples: Jocabel/Abraham story; Menenius Agrippa's fable). When perceived by diegetic listeners, such narratives can have immediate pragmatic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type III relationship: narrating act functions independently of content
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of narrating itself (regardless of the metadiegetic content) performs a diegetic function such as distraction, delay, or obstruction (e.g., Scheherazade's tales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sections where form/performative act (keeping someone alive, stalling, entertaining) is the primary diegetic effect; here the narrating instance's agency and presence grow in importance, often outweighing the actual story content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative metalepsis (transgressive crossings of levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metalepsis encompasses transgressions where boundaries between narrative levels are breached (e.g., extradiegetic intrudes into diegetic world, diegetic characters act on extradiegetic level, inverse cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for authorial intrusions, meta-theatrical moments, or impossible transitions (characters reading/affecting their author, characters becoming readers). Effects are estranging, comic, or fantastic (examples: Sterne, Diderot, Cortazar). Metalepsis is especially notable when narrating acts claim contemporaneity with the story or directly address/alter diegetic events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-diegetic (reduced metadiegetic) technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A form in which a narrative that is second in origin (metadiegetic) is immediately appropriated and told at the first level by the primary narrator, effectively reducing or eliding the intermediary level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify passages where the narrator 'takes the floor' for an embedded narrative, eliminating its reported intermediary; criteria include sudden shifts to the narrator's control, survival of the story but loss of its original speaker. Examples: Plato's Theaetetus (rewording conversation as direct), Proust's pervasive pseudo-diegesis in Recherche where memories/reports are claimed by Marcel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detectability limits: literary vs cinematic markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary texts lack cinematographic devices (blur, slow motion, voice-off) to mark level shifts, so metadiegetic vs pseudo-diegetic status may be ambiguous and hinge on subtle cues like person shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing level shifts, pay attention to grammatical person changes (I → he), explicit attributions of source, memory-prefaces, or editorial signals; absence of such markers can make the metadiegetic status indeterminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative monopoly / unity of instance as a stylistic/narrative choice
rubrics_metrics.description: An author may choose to eliminate metadiegetic narrators and reserve narrating for a single (fictive) author-narrator, thereby creating unity/egocentrism of instance (as in Proust's Recherche).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the narrative voice centralizes narrating authority (monopoly) or distributes it among embedded narrators. Consider effects on narrative control, ego-centrism, and the capacity for other voices to have 'the floor' (e.g., Un amour de Swann is recounted by Marcel rather than Swann).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative as performative / causal force within fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives within the fiction can have performative power to bring about, shape, or trap events (e.g., oracles, fictions that trigger characters' actions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess embedded narratives for their causal/teleological effects on plot (Oedipus' oracle; Scheherazade's tales; Swann's story conditioning Marcel's imagination). Determine whether an embedded narrative functions merely representationally or as an instrument of 'destiny.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Person: homodiegetic vs heterodiegetic distinction (not simple grammar)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary labels 'first-person'/'third-person' are inadequate; instead distinguish homodiegetic narrators (present as characters in the story they tell) from heterodiegetic narrators (absent from the story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the narrator is a character within the narrated events (homodiegetic) or stands outside them (heterodiegetic). Note that presence is a matter of degree (a narrator may be heroically central, marginal, or merely present), and grammatical first-person can denote either genuine character-narration or enunciative presence of the narrating instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelist's choice vs grammatical person
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist chooses a narrative posture (story told by a character vs by an outside narrator); grammatical person (first/third) is an automatic grammatical correlate, not the core narrative decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising writers or analyzing texts, foreground the narrative posture (who is allowed to tell) rather than merely noting grammatical person. This clarifies differences such as Caesar's rhetorical 'we' versus a true character-first-person memoir like Crusoe.
